analysis.one_liner: Directs the Transportation Department to bar airlines from charging fees out of proportion to their actual costs.
analysis.headline: The FAIR Fees Act never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced in December 2021 and died when that Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Transportation to write rules stopping airlines from charging fees — for changing or canceling a ticket, checking a bag, picking a seat, or anything else tied to a flight — that are unreasonable or way out of line with what the airline actually spends to provide the service. It spelled out factors regulators would weigh, like the fact that a canceled seat can usually be resold and that electronic processing costs pennies. It also required airlines to seat families with children 13 or younger together at no extra charge.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers who pay the fees airlines tack onto base fares: change and cancellation charges, checked- and carry-on-bag fees, and seat-selection fees. That includes families who today often pay extra just to guarantee their young children sit next to them, since the bill would require airlines to seat children 13 and under with their family for free. Regulators would have to re-examine the standards every three years, so the relief would be ongoing rather than one-time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers paying bag, change, and seat fees

how_it_helps.text: Within 270 days, the Transportation Secretary would have to write rules prohibiting airlines from imposing any flight-related fee that is unreasonable or disproportional to the costs the airline incurs, covering change and cancellation fees, checked and carry-on bag fees, seat-selection fees, and any other fee tied to a flight.

The rules would have to set standards for judging whether a fee is proportional, looking at what the service actually costs the airline — for example, whether a canceled seat was resold, and the cost of processing a change or a bag electronically plus related labor.

On seat fees specifically, the bill requires that passengers traveling with children age 13 or younger be seated with those children at no additional charge to the family or anyone else on the flight.
The Secretary would have to refresh the standards at least every three years, so the fee limits would keep pace with airline pricing practices.

analysis.who_pays: Passenger airlines, whose ancillary-fee revenue would have to come down wherever a fee exceeds what the service actually costs them. Where a fee was folded into the base fare instead of eliminated, travelers would pay differently but not necessarily less overall.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers 'any other fee imposed by an air carrier relating to a flight' and leaves the reasonableness standards largely to the Transportation Secretary, a broad delegation that could sweep in fees that reflect genuine costs and invite years of litigation over where the line falls.
Airlines could respond by raising base fares to recoup fee revenue rather than absorbing the cut, so travelers who check no bags and change no tickets might end up subsidizing those who do.

Requiring families with young children to be seated together at no charge is a real benefit to those families, but it shifts a cost airlines would otherwise recover onto the fare pool that every passenger shares.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is aimed at fees millions of travelers pay for services that have become very cheap for airlines to provide, and the bill builds in airline-specific cost factors rather than an arbitrary cap, which makes the case for it reasonably strong. The honest cost is that some fee revenue would reappear as higher base fares, spreading costs to travelers who use no optional services, and the open-ended scope could make the rules slow to write and hard to defend in court. On balance the gains to fee-paying travelers look larger than the losses, but the bill was never tested by a hearing or a vote, so its practical design flaws were never worked out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on a December day in 2021 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the Forbidding Airlines from Imposing Ridiculous Fees Act on December 9, 2021, joined by Sens. Blumenthal, Wyden, and Whitehouse.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That referral was the last action of any kind: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines are better off, because they kept collecting change, bag, and seat fees with no cost-proportionality limits. The committee leadership that never scheduled the bill also kept the existing fee system intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, which kept charging unregulated fees

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Fees Act and sponsored it.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration before the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. passenger airline industry
against.what_they_did: Airlines have consistently opposed cost-based limits on change, bag, and seat fees, which are a major revenue source; no airline-group position on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored the bill, but it never got a vote in committee or on the floor, so no one ever had to go on record for or against it.

industries.note: Airlines earn billions of dollars a year from change and cancellation fees, bag fees, and seat-selection fees charged on top of base fares; the bill would force those fees down to roughly the airline's actual cost, and would end the common practice of charging families extra to sit together. The airline's gain and the traveler's cost sit on the same transaction, which is why their interest runs against passengers here.

The bill would not abolish fees, only require them to track actual costs, so airlines could keep charging — just less — and could fold some charges back into ticket prices. Revenue would shrink and pricing would get simpler, but the fee-based business model itself would survive in regulated form.
